k1248: South of Vlorë, real medical infrastructure thins out fast. Sarandë's hospital is genuinely under-resourced, and anything serious means a drive north to Vlorë or Tirana, or — for many residents — a ferry across to Corfu, which has better-equipped facilities within reach in under two hours door to door. This isn't a reason to avoid the Riviera; it's a reason to plan for it directly, particularly for retirees, which is exactly the demographic most drawn to the region in the first place.
k1250: Sarandë's real transport hub isn't an Albanian airport — the region still doesn't have one that flies commercially — it's Corfu's, reached by a ferry that runs 25 to 90 minutes depending on the route, four to six times a day in season, from roughly €10–23. Residents plan flights and visitors around that ferry more than around any drive to Tirana. Road access has genuinely improved: the Llogara tunnel cut the drive from Dukat to Palasë to seven minutes, and Vlorë's bypass has taken most summer traffic off the town centre. Ksamil is the exception worth flagging — a single access road, no real parking infrastructure, and beaches largely fenced off by private beach clubs, all of which make a quiet daily life there harder than the postcard suggests.
k1251: Who's actually settling here, and why
k1252: Italians are the largest foreign group actually moving to the Riviera rather than just buying to rent it out — drawn by the direct ferry link, a familiar climate, and, for a meaningful share of them, retirement. The trade-off they report most often isn't the property itself: it's Albanian bureaucracy, described by more than one Italian buyer as "a comic sketch, but safe" — slow, occasionally chaotic, but not the kind of risk that costs you the property in the end.

k1254: Vlorë and Sarandë are the two towns on this coast that function as places to live year-round rather than places to visit for three months. Everywhere else on the Riviera can still be a good buy — <s1>the investment case for several of these zones is strong</s1> — but "good investment" and "good place to live full-time, day in and day out" are two different questions on this particular stretch of coast, and conflating them is where the disappointment usually starts. k1278: Source: Bank of Albania Housing Price Index, published semi-annually. The deceleration in Tirana across three consecutive releases is the single clearest trend line in the whole dataset — this isn't one soft quarter, it's a slope.
k1279: The uncomfortable number: sales fell while prices rose
k1280: Property sales dropped 35% in 2025, according to the Bank of Albania — while prices kept climbing. That combination, rising price and falling volume, is the textbook signature of a late-cycle market: sellers anchored to last year's number, buyers unwilling to meet it, and fewer transactions clearing at any price. Time on market in Tirana backs it up, stretching from 7.1 months (H2 2024) to 8.1 (H2 2025).
k1281: Underneath both numbers sits the affordability figure that doesn't move quarter to quarter: a Tirana apartment costs roughly <s1>19 years of average gross salary</s1>, against 3–5 years in the EU. That ratio was already the worst recorded in Europe before the slowdown started, which is part of why the slowdown started.

k1298: The lek itself is part of this story and rarely gets mentioned. It has strengthened from roughly 137 to under 98 per euro since 2017 — officially attributed to tourism, remittances and foreign investment, though the IMF has noted the strengthening isn't fully explained by those fundamentals alone, leaving room for informal or illicit inflows as a partial factor. For a euro-denominated buyer, a strong lek means everything priced in local currency — renovation, management, day-to-day costs — has gotten quietly more expensive over the same years prices were rising.

k1317: Two zones on this stretch of coast get all the attention, and both of them are the ones DomLivo's own data flags as overpriced. The better story is the one underneath it — where the same data says the opposite.
k1318: The overpriced case everyone already half-knows: Ksamil
k1319: Ksamil costs more per square metre than Sarandë, its neighbour six kilometres up the coast, and earns less on Airbnb doing it — roughly $5,495 a year against Sarandë's $6,960 — while its listing supply grew 86% in a single year. Higher entry price, lower return, fastest-growing glut on the whole southern coast: if the investment case rests on the numbers alone, they don't support the premium being asked. Layer legal risk on top and it gets worse. Roughly 600 hectares were pulled out of Butrint National Park's buffer zone for development in 2022, UNESCO has formally raised concerns about that and about specific projects built inside it, and enforcement demolitions of unpermitted construction have run in real campaigns since 2010, most recently 2023–2024. A property built in breach of the coastline rules here isn't a fine-and-move-on situation — it's not eligible for legalisation at all.
